transcript:
[Meeting header]
Date: 2026-08-03
Start time: 16:00 UTC
Duration: 48 minutes
Attendees: Elena Park (Redwood AE), Marcus Wu (Redwood SE), Ravi Patel (Sentinel Labs CTO), Maya Gomez (Sentinel Labs Platform), Ibrahim Khan (Sentinel Labs SRE)

Summary: Short intake to map failure modes, SLA commitments and what "degraded" looks like for Sentinel's customer-facing flows. They want decision criteria for Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private and a runbook sketch for regional cordon/failback and cache rehydration. Security and KMS were high priority. Plan to run a small benchmark across two regions with synthetic traffic.

Topics: SLA tiers, multi-region steering, cold vs warm failover, circuit-breakers, KV cache priming, private deployment constraints, audit logs

Action items:
- Redwood to share SOC2 and HSM notes
- Redwood to propose pilot pricing and capacity sizing
- Customer to provide traffic CSV and peak P95 latencies

Transcript:
00:00 Elena Park: Okay, hi everyone, thanks for joining, I'm Elena from Redwood, and with me is Marcus, our systems engineer. how's everyone doing?
00:09 Ravi Patel: Good, thanks. we've got about 45ish minutes right? we've got a couple of folks, I'm Ravi, CTO, Maya is on the platform team and Ibrahim is our SRE lead.
00:20 Marcus Wu: hey all. quick note, I'll be heavy on the topologies and some oscilloscope-y stuff but we'll keep it high level unless you want a deep dive.
00:28 Maya Gomez: that's great, we want to understand real failure modes, like when you say fallback, what actually happens to the user experience and what are the SLA implications.
00:38 Elena Park: perfect, that's exactly what we want to map. quick context from you — are you thinking multi-region active-active or active-passive for your inference layer?
00:47 Ibrahim Khan: right now active-passive looks easier, but we're trying to quantify the latency hit for active-active and cost; our traffic is heavier in US-East but we have EU customers.
00:57 Ravi Patel: also re: data, we need the private option for some customers because of PII, but for most services we could use hosted.
01:05 Marcus Wu: okay, so two main axes: isolation/regulatory (pushes you toward Private/Dedicated) and latency/cost (pushes toward Hosted or Dedicated with region steering). For runbooks, we think in terms of "cordon" and "steer" steps, plus cache rebuild.
01:21 Elena Park: I'll be explicit: cordon means you stop sending new sessions to a region, steering moves traffic to fallback, and rehydrate means the KV cache warm-up — that last one often drives the user-perceived degradation.
01:35 Maya Gomez: can you talk about the difference between warm vs cold standbys in Redwood's offering? like how quickly can a cold pool be spun up?
01:44 Marcus Wu: warm pools are basically maintained active capacity - they hold model weights loaded and kv cache may be primed depending on workload. cold means we allocate VM/GPU and load the model which can be several minutes to tens of minutes depending on model size and quantization. typical numbers: warm standby < 30s for small models with hot caches; cold could be 3-12 mins.
02:06 Ibrahim Khan: 30 seconds vs 3 minutes is a big delta. If we had a canary fallover, can we route a small percentage first and see user impact?
02:15 Elena Park: yes, we support incremental steering and can do traffic split canaries. Redwood Console lets you set canary windows and automatic rollback thresholds if latency or error spikes exceed your SLO.
02:27 Ravi Patel: and in terms of SLA, what do you commit to for hosted vs dedicated? we have enterprise SLAs with penalties so we need guardrails.
02:36 Marcus Wu: hosted has best-effort tiers publicly for self-serve customers; for enterprise we provide Dedicated with SLA-backed uptime and latency buckets. Typical enterprisy SLA language: 99.9% availability for the dedicated pool and SLOs for p95 token latency per model. We can provide regional SLA in contracts.
02:56 Maya Gomez: do you have examples in contracts of partial-degradation allowances, like if we have a 2-minute window of elevated latency during failover is that covered?
03:06 Elena Park: contractually, we define availability by route and model; partial degradation clauses are normalized by objective metrics. The typical approach: define acceptable error budget and scheduled maintenance windows; for emergency failover we have a defined incident classification and we can discuss crediting approach.
03:20 Ibrahim Khan: security question: KMS/HSM — does Redwood support customer-managed keys, and does the private deployment integrate with on-prem HSMs?
03:28 Marcus Wu: yes on Private we integrate with customer KMS/HSM over standard APIs. Hosted supports bring-your-own-key (BYOK) with cloud KMS integrations; on-prem HSM requires Private deployment and additional onboarding.
03:40 Maya Gomez: nice. what about audit logs and traceability? our compliance team insists on tamper-evident logs for inference requests for a subset of customers.
03:48 Elena Park: Redwood Console exposes per-request traces, token-level cost, and you can stream audit logs to a customer's S3/Kafka. We can sign and ship logs, rotation and retention are configurable; for private we can keep full fidelity internally.
03:58 Ravi Patel: ok let me surface an important thing — for our main endpoint, if a region is cordoned we need a deterministic failback timeline and a graceful degradation plan: do you prefer model variant fallbacks (smaller quantized model in fallback region) or queueing requests?
04:15 Marcus Wu: both are patterns we use. model variant fallback means we send to a faster, lower-cost quantized model in fallback region — that reduces compute and keeps latency low but may have quality variance. Queueing increases tail latency. Another hybrid: immediate low-fidelity response with a downstream async more accurate job.
04:34 Ibrahim Khan: is model variant switching automatic or manual?
04:39 Elena Park: you can configure automatic fallbacks with policies: define priority lists, acceptable quality delta, then we can auto-switch if p95 or correctness metrics degrade. It's policy-driven in the Console or via API.
04:52 Maya Gomez: any gotchas with KV caching when you fall back to a different region? keyspace is global for us, do we need to re-prime?
05:00 Marcus Wu: re-prime is the crux. If you have cold-region with empty KV cache, the first wave of requests will miss and incur model compute and higher latency. We recommend prefix caching and proactive priming — Redwood Optimize can suggest which prompts to pre-warm based on traffic patterns.
05:18 Ravi Patel: question on cost — if we do active-active, do we pay for double capacity even if one region is light?
05:24 Marcus Wu: yes active-active implies reserved capacity in both regions. Dedicated pools can offer autoscaling and burst-to-hosted options to reduce cost, but the cost model reflects the standby capacity. For cold standby you pay less because you're not running GPUs.
05:38 Ibrahim Khan: what about network partition scenarios? say inter-region connectivity degraded but both regions up, you might prefer degrading to local cached responses even if some contextual data is missing — can Redwood handle that kind of partial state?
05:51 Marcus Wu: yes we support region-local cache and request-scoped fallbacks; we surface conflict resolution rules. Often customers accept reduced context window in cross-region partitions.
06:05 Maya Gomez: moving to runbooks — can we sketch a simple step-by-step? what does a 5-step runbook look like for a region outage?
06:14 Elena Park: sure — 1) Detect & classify (automated SLO alert), 2) Cordon region (stop new routing), 3) Canary steer 5-10% to target region and measure, 4) Increase steering to 50/100% if health metrics stable, 5) Rehydrate caches and monitor error/latency. Also checkpoint at each step for rollback.
06:34 Ibrahim Khan: do you have automation for steps 2-4?
06:37 Marcus Wu: yes, via policy engine in Redwood Console — you can set thresholds to automate cordon and steering. Or run it manually via API/CLI.
06:47 Ravi Patel: let's talk about SLOs and user experience — we operate a chat+document assistant, intermittent context loss causes user frustration. How do we quantify acceptable quality delta?
06:59 Elena Park: often customers set a functional correctness guardrail: for example a BLEU or Rouge-like metric on a held prompt set; Redwood Optimize can run your prompt suite and surface regressions when a fallback model degrades beyond threshold.
07:15 Maya Gomez: we want to include a human-in-the-loop option — if fallback model quality slips, route requests to a degraded label and surface to escalation queue.
07:23 Marcus Wu: that's supported; you can flag certain prompts and set a higher fidelity path or manual review.
07:29 Ibrahim Khan: any pointers on proving this in a pilot? we want a bench that brakes an edge region and measures p95, error rates and quality delta.
07:38 Elena Park: we'll propose a week-long benchmark: simulate your traffic distribution across US-E, EU, and then force a cordon during peak to measure real observable impact. Marcus will own the plan.
07:48 Marcus Wu: yes I'll scope a script that spins synthetic QPS with a sampled prompt set; we'll capture token latencies, cache hit rates, and quality comparators.
07:57 Ravi Patel: on security, is the telemetry we ship PII-free or does it contain prompt text? we have to be careful.
08:05 Elena Park: by default logs include request hashes and token counts. You can opt-in to full prompt logs for debugging but we treat that as sensitive and pipeline it to your own S3/HSM. For Hosted, we redact by default unless you enable retention.
08:19 Maya Gomez: for Private/Air-gapped deployments, what's the onboarding timeline?
08:24 Marcus Wu: typical Private deployment is 6-12 weeks depending on compliance, network setup, and HSM integration. There's a standard checklist: network peering, KMS configuration, service accounts, and validation runs.
08:36 Ibrahim Khan: do you support SAML SSO and fine-grained RBAC?
08:40 Elena Park: yes, SAML/SSO, OIDC, and RBAC are configurable; we can map to your groups and integrate with SCIM for provisioning.
08:48 Ravi Patel: competitor question — we've evaluated Vendor X and they promised hot failover but their caches were regional-only which caused issues. how is Redwood different?
08:58 Marcus Wu: Redwood's difference is unified runtime and cache-awareness; we support global keyspace with configurable replication strategies and automatic prefix caching. Also we provide policy-driven fallbacks which many vendors lack as integrated features.
09:12 Maya Gomez: any limitations on model types or quantization that affect failover times?
09:16 Marcus Wu: very large models (100B+) will have longer cold start times and may not be practical for cold standby. Quantized models load faster. We'll recommend smaller fallbacks for cross-region to minimize impact.
09:29 Ibrahim Khan: what about legal/procurement red flags — data residency for EU customers, do you offer EU-only deployments?
09:36 Elena Park: yes, we can provision region-restricted Dedicated or Private deployments; hosted offerings also have region isolation options for EU only customers.
09:46 Ravi Patel: ok logistics — can we get a security packet and SOC2 and then a pilot pricing sheet?
09:51 Elena Park: yes I'll send SOC2 and our HSM integration notes. Marcus will send the pilot plan and a proposed benchmark script.
09:59 Marcus Wu: action note: I'll draft the benchmark and runbook and share by next week.
10:05 Maya Gomez: one more question — can we set different fallback policies per endpoint? like search vs chat?
10:12 Elena Park: yes per route policies are supported; you can configure model variant lists, canary windows, and priority regions per endpoint.
10:20 Ibrahim Khan: timeline-wise, we want this pilot to start in two weeks and run for a week.
10:25 Elena Park: sounds doable — we'll try to align schedules after we share the plan.

11:00 (Later portion - clarifications)
11:05 Marcus Wu: clarifying the cache priming — we recommend a two-pronged approach: scheduled priming using top N prompts and reactive priming where early requests are routed to a warm pool for a short period.
11:18 Maya Gomez: reactive priming sounds interesting, does it have cost overhead?
11:21 Marcus Wu: some, but less than running full double capacity. It's a short-lived warm-up cost.
11:28 Ravi Patel: do you have a sample contract clause for partial degradation credits?
11:32 Elena Park: yes we have templates; I'll include an example in the security packet.
11:38 Ibrahim Khan: any examples of customers who've done hot-warm hybrid with cost saving numbers?
11:42 Marcus Wu: we have anonymized case studies; I'll send one where a customer reduced run costs by 28% by using warm standby and autoscaling.

Closing (approx 16:45 UTC)
16:43 Elena Park: great, thanks all. recap: Redwood sends SOC2 + HSM docs, Marcus sends pilot benchmark and runbook, Sentinel shares traffic profile. Plan kickoff for 2026-08-17 (tentative).
16:52 Ravi Patel: thanks, talk soon.
16:54 Maya Gomez: thanks.
16:55 Ibrahim Khan: bye.

Notes on transcription: occasional speaker overlap and mis-heard acronyms (we heard "K V cache" as spelled out). Some product names were paraphrased.
